item.title: Tools I Enjoy Using
item.description:
Being a university student studying both mathematics and computer science, as well as someone who works full time, the tools I use everyday are vital to my success in both school and life. This is even more important for me as I have Bipolar disorder and Autism. Here are some of my favorite tools that I use every day.

Nix

While Homebrew is the conventional pick for a package manager on macOS, I would argue that Nix is the better option. The key reason is reproducability, which means that if I have to wipe my laptop or I get a new machine, I can quickly bootstrap a new system since I have all my settings/options preconfigured. Nix also allows you to manage any Homebrew packages you need, which is my preferred method. The X-Factor of Nix however is that you can specify a “development shell” which contains packages/utilities that you only need for one program, which is great for keeping your machine clean and free from package bulk.

item.title: Is There a Valid Use of AI?
item.description: Recently at my university, there was a controversy over the decision to use a computer-generated voice to read out students names at commencement. While one could take it as an isolated instance, I think we must look at it from a more generalized view of a major problem currently in our society, that is the offloading of parts of the human experience to LLM/Machine Learning platforms such as Claude, Gemini, ElevenLabs, and Nano Banana.

item.title: Terrence Tao Is Right about AI
item.description:
For those of us whose research interests lie at the intersection of Mathematics and Computer Science, most of us have heard of the OpenAI Millennial Prize controversy which erupted violently last week.

For those of us who were living under a rock, on September 7, OpenAI published a paper claiming that they had solved the Navier-Stokes equation on fluid dynamics, one of the Millennium Prize equations as named by the Clay Mathematics Institute. This announcement has courted massive controversy, as OpenAI has been accused by NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster of plagiarizing his and Levent Alpöge’s research work on the equation to make this alleged breakthrough.

item.title: Your Productivity Masturbation Bores Me
item.description:
Like clockwork, around this time every year (right when school starts for those of us in the US/Canada), we see YouTube and social media blow up with people showcasing their “school setups” for maximum producticity. There’s no shortage of all the different softwares, app setups, and other eye candy which they utilitze to showcase how productive they are during the academic year.

It’s all bullshit.

Genuinely, trying to build the perfect productivity setup is a great recipe for never getting anything productive done, because you’ll always be focused on trying to “optimize further”. I’ve written before in a previous blog post about my distain for the San Francisco-style “optimization culture” that is sweeping over Generation Z, but for many people trying to figure out how to get better grades is their first look into this setup.

item.title: The Human Need to Overdo Everything
item.description:
I think that a lot of this “optimization” culture that we’re seeing take over Silicon Valley and the internet is driven by a need to perfect sometime. It’s in our nature as humans to want to overdo something when we get into it. Hell, even I do it. But Silicon Valley takes it to the point where they’ve optimized the enjoyment of life out of it.

Who cares if your health is perfect? Who cares about your alcohol intake? Why did we look at the the hellscape that is companies optimizing our office lives to maximize some value, and go “Yeah, let’s apply that to life”?

item.title: Gostow
item.description: GNU Stow is a great utility, but it’s biggest issue is that it was designed to be general-purpose, meaning there’s some finicky areas where it can mess with your head. One great example is how folder-management is handled. I propose a utility which applies a Suckless philosophy of “do one thing and do it well” for this problem, written in Golang so it compiles as a single binary and not as a Perl module like GNU Stow is.

item.title: How I Take Notes
item.description:
Ever since I downloaded Notion when I first started at community college, I started becoming obsessed with trying to find the ideal note taking system for myself. Early on, I knew that I couldn’t really borrow from someone else’s note taking system, so I began developing my own personal note taking system which is broken into two main parts.

I keep two physical books which I actively write in. The first is a small “Field Notes” journal which I use to jot things down as they come to my in my day-to-day life, and I keep this book on me at all times (work, school, etc). I use this in place of my phone, due to wanting to maintain a clear, easy-to-read system.

item.title: Zettk-CLI
item.description: I find using GUI applications such as Obsidian to be cumbersome and not optimal in some cases for how I take notes and utilize information gathering. A great exmaple is if I just want to make a quick edit to a file. However, I did like some aspects of Obsidian such as templates. I also wanted to develop a system that utilized the Zettelkasten note taking system to it’s fullest, while also learning how to develop CLIs.

item.title: Homelab
item.description: Modern services typically make you choose between having either the convience of a subscription and cloud services, or being able to have control over your personal data. They also don’t mention how you’re at their mercy if they decide to increase the prices of a service. Because of this, I decided to build a home lab to serve as a secure, controlled environment for the data which I don’t want on the cloud.

item.title: The Developer Environment Should Be Disposable
item.description: One of the more common things that us programmers and computer enthusiasts will encounter in our lives is the day we blow up a system. It isn’t a matter of if, but when. I’m pretty sure that once in my life I had to reinstall Windows 10 five times in one week, because I kept thinking I could mess around with the registry editor and improve the performance of my computer “just a little more”, and then boom: It would stop booting to save my life.
